How many ways can you select 6 numbers from 0 to 99 if the order does not matter? If the order does not matter, this is a combination problem. The formula for combinations is C(n, k) = n! / (k!(n-k)!), where n is the total number of items, k is the number of items to choose, and "!" denotes factorial. In this case, n = 100 (since we're choosing from 0 to 99) and k = 6. So, C(100, 6) = 1,192,052,400 (~1.2 billion) possible combinations.

And how many ways if the order does matter? If the order matters, this is a permutation problem. The formula for permutations is P(n, k) = n! / (n-k)!, where n is the total number of items, and k is the number of items to choose. In this case, n = 100 and k = 6. So, P(100, 6) = 858,277,728,000 (~858.3 billion) possible permutations.
